strengths: Clear motivation and problem identification: The paper effectively articulates why RL is well-suited for C-STS (direct optimization of non-differentiable Spearman metric) and convincingly demonstrates why naive listwise RL fails through empirical evidence (Figure 1)

Strong empirical results with comprehensive benchmarking: Achieves SOTA on C-STS (48.18 Spearman), outperforms proprietary models (GPT-4o by 3.95 points), and demonstrates impressive small-model performance (0.6B model outperforms GPT-4)
Innovative PSRR mechanism: The parallel slice ranking reward is a clever solution to the credit assignment problem in batch-level ranking, enabling fine-grained differentiated learning signals

Thorough experimental validation: Extensive ablation studies (Tables 2-4), comprehensive hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (Tables 3, 7-9), error distribution analysis, qualitative case studies, and validation on re-annotated dataset demonstrate robustness
Two-stage curriculum design is well-motivated: Progressing from simple pointwise objectives to complex hybrid rewards effectively manages learning complexity and prevents training collapse
Strong reproducibility support: Detailed hyperparameter configurations, complete prompt templates, promise of code release, and clear methodological descriptions facilitate reproduction
Generalization across model scales: Shows consistent improvements across 0.6B, 4B, and 8B models, suggesting the approach is not scale-dependent
Technical soundness: Standard RL formulation with clear MDP definition, proper advantage computation via Z-score normalization, and well-specified loss functions
weaknesses: Limited novelty in RL methodology: The paper primarily applies existing DAPO algorithm with standard reward components (pointwise, pairwise, listwise). Main contributions (two-stage scheduling and PSRR) are relatively straightforward applications of known techniques, not fundamental algorithmic advances. No exploration of alternative RL algorithms on this task.

Unfair experimental comparisons: GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1 are evaluated only in few-shot mode without fine-tuning. A fair comparison would involve fine-tuning these models, making it unclear whether improvements stem from RL effectiveness or specialized task adaptation

Overclaimed generalizability: PSRR is tested on only one additional task (WMT-QE). Single-task transfer is insufficient to support claims of being a 'generalizable strategy' for ranking tasks. Pairwise rewards exploit C-STS's paired structure, and binary rewards target task-specific label boundaries

Insufficient analysis of PSRR mechanism: Optimal slice size N=24 is identified but limited guidance provided for other tasks. No computational complexity analysis, runtime comparisons, or theoretical justification for the mechanism's design

Missing baseline comparisons: Authors' own SFT implementations used—unclear if these match published SEAVER or if other SFT approaches would be stronger. No comparison of different RL algorithms (PPO, GRPO variants) on C-STS

Incomplete technical documentation: Gradient accumulation strategy mentioned but not detailed regarding its effect on results. Score extraction logic (Parse function) not fully specified. No analysis of training stability, convergence properties, or failure modes
No statistical significance testing: Reported improvements lack confidence intervals or significance tests, making it unclear if differences are statistically meaningful

Computational overhead not fully addressed: Using 8 completions and gradient accumulation has significant memory/compute costs, but wall-clock time comparisons with SFT baselines are not provided. Practical applicability unclear without efficiency analysis

strengths: Strong empirical results on C-STS benchmark (48.18 Spearman), with consistent improvements across model sizes and outperformance of proprietary models
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including detailed ablations (Table 2), sensitivity analyses, re-annotated dataset validation, and comparison with differentiable objectives
Clear problem motivation with empirical evidence for why naive listwise RL fails, and good presentation of the method
Effective demonstration that smaller fine-tuned models can outperform much larger zero-shot proprietary models, suggesting optimization benefits beyond scale
Demonstrates efficiency across model sizes (0.6B outperforms GPT-4)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: two-stage curriculum is standard RL practice; pointwise/pairwise/listwise rewards are well-established in ranking; PSRR is primarily a straightforward batching/data organization strategy rather than a conceptual advance

PSRR mechanism lacks mechanistic justification: why slice size N=24 is optimal is purely empirical; the mechanism appears sensitive to this hyperparameter; no theoretical or intuitive explanation for why per-sample signals fundamentally outperform batch-level signals beyond engineering convenience

Unfair experimental comparisons: fine-tuned 8B model compared against zero-shot few-shot proprietary models (GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1); SEAVER baseline is discriminative 355M vs generative 8B; no comparison with other RL algorithms (PPO, DPO) using same reward structure

Suspicious naive RL baseline: achieves only 38.19 vs 37.90 few-shot (+0.29), suggesting potentially suboptimal implementation; proper DAPO baseline with batch-level listwise rewards would be more convincing

Overstated generalization claims: WMT-QE test uses minimalist configuration removing C-STS-specific components; only 3.43 point gain vs 10.35 on C-STS; only one additional task tested; method deeply coupled with C-STS's paired structure

Missing reproducibility details: code URL is blank; prompt sensitivity not evaluated; training duration and convergence criteria not specified; computational cost vs SFT not provided; no confidence intervals or significance testing
Narrow scope: C-STS is a recent niche task (2023); method is task-specific; experiments only on Qwen3 family; limited to discriminative cross-encoder paradigm without exploring other architectures

Insufficient mechanistic insights: why does two-stage training work beyond empirical results? What does the model learn differently in Stage II? Gradient flow analysis or loss landscape visualization would strengthen understanding; case study is single cherry-picked example

strengths: First successful application of RL to C-STS with LLM-based cross-encoder, addressing a clear research gap
Strong empirical results: achieves 48.18 Spearman (SOTA for cross-encoder), outperforms GPT-4o (+3.95) and DeepSeek-R1 (+5.33 points)
Innovative PSRR mechanism cleverly solves the credit assignment problem through parallel slice decomposition, enabling granular learning signals
Comprehensive experimental validation including thorough ablation studies, sensitivity analyses, error distribution analysis, and qualitative case studies
Well-motivated two-stage curriculum with clear progression from foundational (pointwise + binary) to refined (hybrid) objectives
Demonstrates generalization to WMT-QE task and notably shows compact 0.6B model (44.34) outperforming GPT-4 (43.6), suggesting gains from alignment rather than scale
Good reproducibility efforts with promised code release, detailed prompt templates, and comprehensive hyperparameter configurations
Performance validated on re-annotated C-STS dataset confirming gains are not due to label noise overfitting
weaknesses: Lacks theoretical justification for why naive listwise RL fails or why the proposed PSRR decomposition is optimal; design appears somewhat ad-hoc

Limited generalization evidence: only one out-of-domain evaluation (WMT-QE) using 'minimalist configuration'; pairwise reward exploits C-STS's paired structure, raising questions about applicability to unpaired data
Incomplete baseline comparisons: proprietary models only evaluated in few-shot settings; unclear if fine-tuning would close the gap; SFT baseline (40.42 for 8B) appears surprisingly weak
Introduces 9 hyperparameters (λ₁, λ₂, λ₃, μ₁, μ₂, μ₃, R_base, G, N) requiring careful tuning, potentially limiting practical adoption
Missing critical details: no computational cost analysis, no statistical significance testing (no error bars or confidence intervals), no discussion of failure modes or convergence behavior
Dramatic gap between original (48.18 Spearman) and re-annotated (76.08 Spearman) dataset scores raises concerns about original benchmark reliability and label quality
Limited theoretical novelty: two-stage curriculum is established, individual reward components are standard, main novelty (PSRR) is incremental
Insufficient analysis of why RL benefits small models disproportionately or how the method scales with model size and dataset characteristics
